question: A 70-year-old man presents at 3 a.m. with sudden inability to pass urine for 10 hours, severe suprapubic pain, and a grossly distended, tender bladder on examination. What is the immediate priority?

answers.text: Administer oral tamsulosin and review in four hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Alpha-blockers may help prevent acute retention but do not relieve an existing obstruction; the patient needs immediate decompression, not medical therapy.

answers.text: Insert a urethral catheter to drain the bladder immediately

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Acute painful urinary retention requires immediate bladder decompression by urethral catheterisation. Relief of pain is instant and prevents obstructive renal damage.

answers.text: Arrange a transrectal ultrasound of the prostate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diagnostic imaging is not the priority in a symptomatic emergency; decompression must come first, investigation can follow once the patient is comfortable.

answers.text: Measure PSA and request a urology outpatient appointment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PSA measurement is elective and inappropriate in the acute setting — acute urinary retention is a surgical emergency requiring immediate catheterisation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Acute urinary retention with a distended, painful bladder is a surgical emergency. Catheterisation is the immediate priority; investigation and treatment of the underlying cause comes after decompression.
Correct. Acute painful retention — catheterise immediately. Everything else follows once the bladder is drained.
